name: Finjuve topical finasteride

lead: Finjuve is a brand name for topical finasteride, a spray form of the drug used to treat androgenetic alopecia (male pattern hair loss). Finasteride blocks conversion of testosterone to DHT, the hormone linked to follicle miniaturization.

The appeal is a hair-retention and regrowth treatment applied to the scalp rather than swallowed, which is designed to limit exposure elsewhere in the body. A phase III trial of a topical finasteride spray in men with androgenetic alopecia has been published.

paras: It is a prescription product applied to the scalp as a spray, typically as part of a routine alongside other hair-loss treatments, and prescribed by a clinician. Hair-loss treatments generally take months to show effect.

Topical finasteride, like oral, reduces serum DHT. Reported side effects of oral finasteride include sexual effects; whether topical use differs is still being studied. Finasteride is not for use by women who are or may become pregnant.

angle.text: Applied to the scalp as a spray, it targets the same hormone pathway as oral finasteride to keep and thicken hair at the hairline and crown.

lead: Finjuve is a topical finasteride spray for male androgenetic alopecia. Finasteride is a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor; oral 1 mg finasteride (Propecia) is an established treatment for male pattern hair loss that slows loss, and meta-analyses cited by Wikipedia report about 15 percent regrowth.[1]

Topical formulations are designed to minimize systemic exposure by acting on the hair follicles themselves, although topical finasteride, like oral, lowers serum DHT.[1] A 2022 phase III randomized controlled trial of a topical finasteride spray in men with androgenetic alopecia was published in the Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology.[1] Earlier studies from 2018 and 2020 described topical finasteride's preliminary effectiveness.[1]

paras: It is used for male pattern hair loss. Oral finasteride is the established form; topical formulations have preliminary-to-growing evidence.[1]
Finasteride inhibits type II 5-alpha-reductase, reducing DHT. Topical forms aim to concentrate effect in the scalp, but serum DHT reduction has been measured with topical use.[1]
The adverse effects reviewed for finasteride are mainly for the oral drug, and they should not be assumed to apply equally to topical use.[1]

A phase III randomized controlled trial of a topical finasteride spray in male androgenetic alopecia (Piraccini et al., 2022) and earlier studies from 2018 and 2020 are cited in the Wikipedia finasteride article, which does not report their detailed results.[1]

timeline.event: Phase III trial of topical finasteride spray published.[1]
